analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans, Medicaid, Medicare, TRICARE, and VA to cover IVF and other fertility treatment.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 by Sen. Cory Booker with six Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every kind of health coverage in the country — private insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, federal employee plans, military coverage, and veterans' care — to pay for fertility treatment, including IVF, whenever the plan already covers pregnancy care. It would cap what patients can be charged out of pocket for that treatment and bar insurers from discouraging or penalizing it. Introduced by Sen. Cory Booker in July 2025, it has not moved since it was sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People trying to have a child who currently pay fertility care out of pocket — a single IVF cycle commonly costs five figures. This includes employees whose plans exclude IVF, veterans and their spouses or partners (whose fertility coverage is now very limited), Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries, military families, and federal workers. The bill covers treatment regardless of whether the person has a formal infertility diagnosis, and limits cost-sharing to what the plan charges for other medical services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who can't afford fertility treatment

how_it_helps.text: Requires any group or individual health plan that covers pregnancy (obstetrical) care to also cover fertility treatment — including IVF, insemination, egg/sperm/embryo preservation, embryo genetic testing, gamete donation, and fertility medications — whether or not the patient has been diagnosed with infertility.
Bars plans from charging higher deductibles, coinsurance, or other limits for fertility treatment than they charge for other medical services.

Prohibits insurers from offering patients incentives to skip treatment, gagging doctors from discussing it, or cutting a provider's reimbursement for providing it, and applies federal anti-discrimination law to the new coverage.
Extends coverage to federal employees' plans (FEHB), military families (TRICARE), and veterans and their spouses or partners through the VA.
Makes fertility treatment a mandatory Medicaid benefit that states must cover, and adds it to Medicare with Medicare paying the full allowed charge and waiving the deductible.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers and the employers who fund most group plans would absorb the cost of a new required benefit, which typically gets passed back to everyone through higher premiums. Taxpayers would fund the expansions through Medicaid (shared federal-state), Medicare, TRICARE, and the VA. States may need to pass legislation to comply, and the bill gives them extra time to do so.

drawbacks.text: The private-plan mandate is unfunded: there is no payment to insurers or employers, so the added cost of an expensive benefit would most likely show up in premiums paid by all enrollees, including people who will never use fertility care.
The requirement only kicks in if a plan already covers pregnancy services, which leaves a loophole: a plan could drop obstetrical coverage to avoid covering fertility treatment.

Coverage applies regardless of an infertility diagnosis, and nothing in the bill caps the number of treatment cycles, so total spending on the new benefit is open-ended and no cost estimate accompanies the bill in the record.
The public side — Medicaid and Medicare — is entirely taxpayer-funded, so the federal and state budgets would take on recurring new spending with no offset in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people priced out of having a child, the benefit is direct and large: coverage for treatments that today often cost more than a year's salary per attempt. The costs are real but diffuse — higher premiums spread across everyone with employer or individual insurance, and new federal and state spending on Medicaid and Medicare. The bill's design has genuine gaps (the pregnancy-coverage trigger creates an escape hatch, and the no-diagnosis, no-cycle-limit breadth makes costs hard to predict), and the record contains no cost estimate to weigh against the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles health bills, where it has sat for months without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on July 23, 2025.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee.
Six Senate Democrats have signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has.
Since the referral, the action record shows no committee hearing, no markup, and no vote of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet. If the bill stays parked in committee, insurers and employers avoid a new required benefit, while people who need fertility care keep paying for it themselves — a single IVF cycle commonly runs five figures out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill hasn't moved

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its sole sponsor.

for.name: 6 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chairs has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred on July 23, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors are Senate Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-chaired HELP Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would make these clinics the paid channel for a newly guaranteed benefit across nearly all insurance, giving them a large insured patient base with no new competition attached. Their gain and patients' gain point the same way here.

Insurers would have to add an expensive mandatory benefit to any plan that covers pregnancy, though the bill lets them negotiate provider reimbursement and they can push much of the cost into premiums. Their financial interest runs against the mandate that patients would benefit from.
Most workers' coverage is employer-funded, so the new required benefit lands on employers' benefit budgets, with collective bargaining agreements given extra time before compliance.
The bill explicitly requires coverage of fertility medications, prescribed or over the counter, creating insured demand for their products.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to Senate committee never get a hearing or vote, and this one shows the usual warning signs: no Republican cosponsors, no committee action in the months since referral, and a HELP Committee controlled by the other party. Unless it is folded into a larger health package — for which there is no sign in the record — it is likely to die quietly when this Congress ends in early January 2027.
